Army and garrison commissioners and vice commissioners served four-year terms; commanders-in-chief and below, two years; escort officers rotated with their units. Chief and vice commissioners and officers below them had attendants, separately listed on memorials. On visits to the three capitals, southern and northern Eastern Capital guards each gained Left and Right Encampments under separate commissioners. When the emperor was in the capital, the capital guard followed the same arrangement. A great general on campaign reported to the temples, received the axes, took leave at the Grand Duke of Qi's temple, and did not sleep at home. In the field he might punish soldiers who disobeyed orders without further reference. After victory, before disbanding, he mustered the army, recorded merit and costs, and reported to the Grand Temple. A triumphant field marshal was always greeted with suburban ceremony. The responsible office first offered the victory at the Grand Temple, then at the Grand Duke of Qi's temple. One vice director handled tribute examinations and miscellaneous petitions. Tribute examinations were held each early spring together with the annual account submission. There were two subjects: level shooting and military examination. Subject standing and merit grades were verified before appointment. One vice director adjudicated the Southern Bureau. Annual candidates presented discharge papers, registers, qualifications, and performance records. They passed through this office for verification before proceeding to the Three Bureaus. Candidates advanced to Grade A received endorsement. Directorate of Operations Director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Director of Territories. Vice director: one post, upper primary sixth rank. Section heads: two persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Four record clerks, nine document record clerks, and four custodians. The director and vice director maintained empire maps and counts of walls, moats, garrisons, and beacons, and tracked distances and barbarian submission. They adjudicated the five regions, changes of capitals, and border disputes. Upper garrisons numbered twenty, middle ninety, and lower one hundred thirty-five empire-wide. Upper frontier posts eleven, middle eighty-six, lower two hundred forty-five. Beacon towers were generally placed about thirty li apart. Along the frontier they built walled posts for the beacons. Each beacon station had one commander and one deputy. Prefectural and county gates and granary gates required garrison guards. Directorate of Equipage Director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Director of Carriages. Vice director: one post, upper secondary sixth rank. Section heads: three persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Ten record clerks, twenty document record clerks, and four custodians. They kept registers of imperial and official transport, relay stations, stables, and livestock, and controlled receipts and issues. Posts stood every thirty li—one thousand six hundred thirty-nine empire-wide—with sixty-five supervisory pastures under regional commissioners. Breeding standards and herd counts were recorded under the Imperial Stud. Guards kept standing-duty horses and offices reserve transport oxen, with numbers fixed by regulation. Directorate of the Armory Director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Director of Storehouses. Vice director: one post, upper secondary sixth rank. Section heads: two persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Seven record clerks, fifteen document record clerks, and four custodians. The director and vice director managed weapons and ceremonial regalia for military prefectures empire-wide. They tracked issue and receipt of ceremonial displays, sacrificial goods, and funeral equipment, measured repair and manufacture, and distributed items. Minister of Justice: one post, upper primary third rank. Early Sui renamed the post Director of the Capital Office; it later became Ministry of Justice. Longshuo made it Grand Constant of Punishments; Guangzai, Autumn Office Minister; Shenlong restored the former title. Vice minister: one post. Upper primary fourth rank, lower grade. Under Longshuo it was Vice Grand Constant of Punishments. The minister and vice minister oversaw criminal law, convict labor, case review, and frontier pass control empire-wide. Four subordinate offices: Punishments, Capital Office, Comparison, and Gate. They coordinated duties and executed regulations. Matters from all inner and outer offices passed through their subordinates for verification. Punishments Bureau directors: two posts, upper secondary fifth rank. Sui called it Statutes Bureau director; Wude, Punishments Bureau director; Longshuo, Director of Punishments. Vice directors: two posts, upper secondary sixth rank. Section heads: four persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Nineteen record clerks, thirty-eight document record clerks, six station chiefs, and ten custodians. Directors and vice directors assisted the minister, applied the code, and distinguished severity. Written law had four forms: lü, ling, ge, and shi. Lü comprised twelve chapters—from General Provisions through Trial and Sentence—totaling five hundred articles. Ling: twenty-seven sections in thirty scrolls. The twenty-seven ling sections—from grades and posts through miscellaneous ling—contained one thousand five hundred forty-six articles. Ge: twenty-four sections. Shi: thirty-three sections. They were organized under the ministries, Censorate, nine courts, three directorates, and armies. Lü defined crimes and fixed punishments. Ling set administrative models and systems. Ge forbade violations and corrected deviance. Shi gauged things and measured procedures. Punishments were graded in five: beating, flogging, penal servitude, exile, and death. Beating and flogging each had five degrees, penal servitude five, exile three, death two. Trial and sentence rested on the Ten Abominations, Eight Deliberations, Five Hearings, and Six Categories of Graft. Redemption and assignment are set out in the Treatise on Punishment Law. All death sentences required detailed review by the Secretariat and Chancellery. Capital convicts wore cangue and fetters. Women and exiles or penal servants wore cangue only. Officials of seventh rank or above, or with merit or scatter grades, were chained but not cangued. In the capital, penal servitude and above went to Judicial Review; flogging and below were decided by the home office. Prisoners seized by the Golden Crow Guard were also sent to Judicial Review. In the capital, capital sentences required five review memorials from the executing office; outside the capital, three review memorials from the Ministry of Justice. Rebellious treason and household retainers or slaves who killed their master required only one review memorial. Execution days in the capital required reduced meals and silenced music. Capital punishment was forbidden from after spring establishment until the autumn equinox. The same rule applied on great sacrifices, abstention days, new and full moons, quarter moons, the twenty-four qi, rain before clearing, night before dawn, meat-abstention periods, and holidays. Offenders guilty of exile or below who merited dismissal from office— if they died before memorial was submitted, posthumous dismissal and confiscation were waived. Exiles might not abandon wife or concubine or steal home in secret. After six years they might resume office. If exile was specially assigned though the crime did not warrant it, office was permitted after three years. Penal servitude was served as assigned residence labor. Imprisoned convicts were reviewed every five days. Examining officers related to or at enmity with the accused were replaced on request. Capital offices reported prisoners to Justice by the twenty-fifth of each month; on amnesty day convicts were assembled at the palace gate, the golden rooster was raised, and release followed the proclamation. Capital Office director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Longshuo renamed it Director of Retainers; Xianheng restored the former title. Vice director: one post, upper secondary sixth rank. Section heads: two persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Four record clerks, twelve document record clerks, and four custodians. They assigned convict labor, supplied captives and convicts with clothing, grain, and medicine, and heard suits to redress injustice. They maintained full knowledge of free and bonded persons, public and private. Collective guilt for rebellion or treason confiscated the household as government slave women. One amnesty made them frontier households; a second, miscellaneous households; a third restored free status, as the amnesty provided. At sixty with disability they became frontier households even if uncovered by amnesty; at seventy free persons, registered where they chose. On first confiscation, skilled persons were assigned to offices matching their ability. Craftswomen entered the Palace Domestic Service. The unskilled were assigned to the Imperial Granaries. Comparison Bureau director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo it was Director of Accounts. Vice director: one post, upper secondary sixth rank. Section heads: two persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Fourteen record clerks. Twenty-seven document record clerks, one accounting clerk, and four custodians. They audited salaries, office costs, fines, levies, convict labor, tax quotas, and arrears empire-wide and reconciled all expenditures. Inner and outer officials received salaries graded by rank. Outer officials' pay varied with upper, middle, or lower prefecture, county, or seat. Household tax supplied prefectural and county monthly salaries from interest on office capital. Han officials in suzerain prefectures were paid in local goods. Pass and barrier officials were paid by rank. They received light goods as annual payment. Garrison marshals and adjutants received capital-grade salaries. Garrison and frontier pay varied with upper, middle, or lower garrison grade. The capital held separate grain-loan capital reported quarterly; prefectures reported yearly—Comparison Bureau audited all. They also audited granaries, palace stores, construction, hired labor, craftsmen, work quotas, fines, levies, rewards, gifts, military funds, weapons, grain purchases, and garrison herds. Gate Office director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo it was Director of the Gate Office. Vice director: one post, upper secondary sixth rank. Section heads: two persons, upper secondary ninth rank. Six record clerks, thirteen document record clerks, and four custodians. They kept registers and transit levies for all passes and barriers and supervised their administration. Passes numbered twenty-six, divided upper, middle, and lower. Capital passes on relay routes were upper passes. Other passes on relay routes, or on the four sides without relay routes, were middle passes. All others were lower passes. Passes separated inner from outer and Chinese from barbarian, using terrain as barrier and barring forbidden traffic. Passes inspected traffic without routine levy, controlled goods in transit, confiscated contraband, and fined offenders. Travelers obtained a transit permit from their home office—the ministry in the capital, the prefecture outside. Even outside their jurisdiction, local authorities issued permits when a document arrived from another office. Ministry of Works: one Minister of Works, positive third rank. Under the Southern Dynasties the office was called Works Initiation. When major construction was needed, a Minister of Works Initiation was appointed and abolished once the work was done. The Sui at its founding reestablished the Minister of Works. Longshuo renamed it Grand Steward of Equilibrium Director; Guangde made it Winter Office Minister; Shenlong restored the old title. One vice minister. Lower positive fourth rank. Under Longshuo it became Vice Grand Steward of Equilibrium. The minister and vice minister held empire-wide authority over craftsmen, garrison fields, mountains, and marshes. Four subordinate bureaus: Works, Garrison Fields, Parks, and Waterways. They summarized their duties and executed imperial orders. All central and local bureau affairs under their jurisdiction were authenticated by them. Works Bureau director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Grandee of Equilibrium. One vice director, upper secondary sixth rank. Two section heads, upper secondary ninth rank. Twelve record clerks, twenty-one document record clerks, six station chiefs, and eight custodians. Directors and vice directors oversaw the many tasks of planning and construction. They measured and planned repair of walls and moats, upkeep of earthworks and timber, and craftsmen's standards. Construction at the capital and eastern capital was assigned to the Palace Workshops and Directorate of Works. Garrison Fields Bureau director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Grandee of Fields. One vice director, upper secondary sixth rank. Two section heads, upper secondary ninth rank. Seven record clerks, twelve document record clerks, one accounting clerk, and four custodians. Directors and vice directors held empire-wide authority over garrison-field policy. When frontier garrisons could not be fed by transport, garrison fields were set up to augment army stores. They decided fertility of land and water, suitable crops, labor quotas, and harvest grades. Every garrison field had fixed labor quotas. Military prefectures empire-wide administered nine hundred ninety-two garrison fields. Large fields were fifty qing; small ones twenty qing. Each garrison graded its land good, middling, or poor and its harvests rich or lean in three tiers. Every garrison field had a garrison officer and a deputy. Capital civil and military officials with duty-fields held land tied to their posts. Jingzhao, Henan, and capital county officials followed the same rule. Capital offices with public-hall fields received allotments scaled to rank. Parks Bureau director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Grandee of Parks. One vice director, upper secondary sixth rank. Two section heads, upper secondary ninth rank. Four record clerks, nine document record clerks, and four custodians. Directors and vice directors oversaw planting in capital streets, mountain parks and preserves, vegetation, fuel, progress supplies, and hunting grounds. Gathering, hunting, and fishing had to follow the seasons. Around Jingzhao and Henan, four suburban zones and three hundred li were barred to hunting and gathering. Idle-stable horses of the Palace Service and Imperial Stud drew fodder from within five hundred li of both capitals. Pasture offices in Guannei, Longyou, and western and southern missions stored hay and forage for livestock. Firewood, charcoal, and timber for the palace, officials, and foreign guests were collected in agricultural slack seasons. Waterways Bureau director: one post, upper secondary fifth rank. Under Longshuo the title was Grandee of Rivers. One vice director, upper secondary sixth rank. Two section heads, upper secondary ninth rank. Four record clerks, nine document record clerks, and four custodians. Directors and vice directors governed rivers, marshes, and reservoirs, opened canals, and dammed and repaired waterways. They tallied and promoted every benefit from shipping, irrigation, and drainage. The realm counted three hundred twenty-two thousand three hundred fifty-nine water sources. Sources in remote borderlands beyond reach could not be known. The Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, from the west to the eastern sea, were China's great rivers. One hundred thirty-five other waters were middle rivers. Another one thousand two hundred fifty-two were small rivers. The Wei, Luo, Fen, Ji, Zhang, Qi, Huai, and Han linked distant regions, carried merchant fleets, and sustained the people from abundance to scarcity. The realm had four boat bridges: Pujin, Dayang, and Heyang on the Yellow River, and Xiaoyi on the Luo. Four stone-pier bridges: Tianjin, Yongji, and Zhongqiao on the Luo, and Ba Bridge on the Ba. Three timber-pier bridges on the Wei: Bian Bridge, Central Wei Bridge, and Eastern Wei Bridge. Eleven great bridges were repaired by state craftsmen. The rest were maintained as needed by responsible prefectures and counties. Major crossings without bridges were served by ferrymen, graded by craft size and difficulty.

=門下省=秦、漢初，置侍中，曾無台省之名。 自晉始置門下省，南、北朝皆因之。 龍朔改為東台，光宅改為鸞台，神龍復。 侍中侍中二員。 隋曰納言，又名侍內。 武德為納言，又改為侍中。 龍朔改東台左相，光宅元年改為納言，神龍復為侍中。 開元元年改為黃門監，五年復為侍中。 天寶二年改為左相。 至德二年復改為侍中。 武德定令，侍中正三品，大曆二年十一月九日，升為正二品。 舊制，宰相常于門下省議事，謂之政事堂。 永淳二年七月，中書令裴炎以中書執政事筆，遂移政事堂於中書省。 開元十一年，中書令張說改政事堂為中書門下，其政事印，改為中書門下之印也。 侍中之職，掌出納帝命，緝熙皇極，總典吏職，贊相禮儀，以和萬邦，以弼庶務，所謂佐天子而統大政者也。 凡軍國之務，與中書令參而總焉，坐而論之，舉而行之，此其大較也。 凡下之通上，其制有六：一曰奏抄，二曰奏彈，三曰露布，四曰議，五曰表，六曰狀； 皆審署申覆而施行焉。 凡法駕行幸，則負寶而從。 大朝會、大祭祀，則板奏中嚴外辦，以為出入之節。 輿駕還宮，則請解嚴，所以告禮成也。 凡大祭祀，皇帝致齋，既朝，則請就齋室。 將奠，則奉玉及幣以進。 盥手，則取匜以沃。 洗爵，則酌罍水以奉。 及贊酌泛齊，進福酒以成其禮焉。 若享宗廟，則進瓚而贊酌鬱酒以稞。 既稞，則贊酌醴齊。 其餘如饗神祇之禮。 藉田，則奉耒以贊事。 凡諸侯王及四夷之君長朝見，則承詔而勞問之。 臨軒命使，冊後及太子，則承詔以命之。 凡制敕慰問外方之臣及徵召者，則監其封題。 若發驛遣使，則給其傳符，以通天下之信。 凡官爵廢置，刑政損益，皆授之於記事之官。 既書於策，則監其記注焉。 凡文武職事六品已下，所司進擬，則量其階資，校其才用，以審定之。 若擬職不當，隨其優屈，退而量焉。 門下侍郎門下侍郎二員。 隋曰黃門侍郎。 龍朔為東台侍郎，咸亨改為黃門侍郎，垂拱改為鸞台侍郎，天寶二年改為門下侍郎，乾元元年改為黃門侍郎，大曆二年四月復為門下侍郎。 武德定令，中書門下侍郎，同尚書侍郎，正四品上。 大曆二年九月敕升為正三品也。 門下侍郎掌貳侍中之職。 凡政之弛張，事之與奪，皆參議焉。 若大祭祀，則從升壇以陪禮。 皇帝盥手，則奉巾以進。 既帨，則奠巾於篚，奉瓠爵以贊獻。 凡元正、冬至天子視朝，則以天下祥瑞奏聞。 給事中給事中四員。 正五品上。 隋曰給事郎，置四員，位次門下侍郎。 武德定令，曰給事中。 龍朔改為東台舍人，咸亨復。 給事中掌陪侍左右，分判省事。 凡百司奏抄，侍中審定，則先讀而署之，以駁正違失。 凡制敕宣行，大事則稱揚德澤，褒美功業，覆奏而請施行； 小事則署而頒之。 凡國之大獄，三司詳決，若刑名不當，輕重或失，則援法例退而裁之。 凡發驛遣使，則審其事宜，與黃門侍郎給之； 其緩者給傳，即不應給，罷之。 凡文武六品已下授職官，所司奏擬，則校其仕曆淺深，功狀殿最，訪其德行，量其才藝； 若官非其人，理失其事，則白侍中而退量焉。 若弘文館圖書之繕寫、讎校，亦課而察之。 凡天下冤滯未申及官吏刻害者，必聽其訟，與御史、中書舍人同計其事宜，而申理之。 錄事錄事四人，從七品上。 主事四人，從八品下。 令史十一人，書令史二十二人，甲庫令史七人，傳制八人，亭長六人，掌固十人，修補制敕匠五人。 左散騎常侍左散騎常侍二人。 從三品。 魏、晉置散騎常侍、侍郎，與侍中、黃門侍郎共平尚書奏事。 其後用人或雜，江左不重此官，或省或置。 隋初省散騎侍郎，置常侍四人，從三品，掌陪從朝直。 煬帝又省之。 武德初，以為加官。 貞觀初，置常侍二人，隸門下省。 明慶二年，又置二員，隸中書省，始有左右之號，並金蟬珥貂。 左常侍與侍中左貂，右常侍與中書令右貂，謂之八貂。 龍朔為左侍極，咸亨復。 廣德二年五月，升為正三品，加置四員。 興元元年正月，左右各加一員。 貞元四年正月敕，依舊四員也。 常侍掌侍奉規諷，備顧問應對。 寶應二年敕，左右散騎常侍各置參官兩人，令自揀擇聞奏，參典亦置兩人，後省。 諫議大夫諫議大夫四員。 秦、漢曰諫大夫，光武加議字。 隋于門下省置諫議大夫七員，從四品下。 武德四年敕置四員，正五品上。 龍朔改為正諫大夫，神龍復。 大曆四年敕只四員，正五品上。 龍朔七年三月敕，其諫議四員，內供奉不得為正員。 至貞元四年五月十五日敕，諫議分為左右，加置八員，四員隸門下為左，會昌二年十一月中書奏：隋于門下省置諫議大夫七員，從四品下。 今正五品上。 自大曆二年門下中書侍郎升為正三品，兩省遂闕四品官。 其諫議大夫望升為正四品下，分為左右，以備兩省四品之闕。 向後與丞郎出入迭用，以重其選。 敕可之。 諫議大夫掌侍從贊相，規諫諷諭。 凡諫有五：一曰諷諫，二曰順諫，三曰規諫，四曰致諫，五曰直諫。 起居郎起居郎二員，從六品上。 古無其名，隋始置起居舍人二員。 貞觀二年省起居舍人，移其職于門下，置起居郎二員。 明慶中又置起居舍人，始與起居郎分在左右。 龍朔二年改為左史，咸亨復。 天授元年又改為左史，神龍復也。 楷書手三人。 起居郎掌起居注，錄天子之言動法度，以修記事之史。 凡記事之制，以事系日，以日系月，以月系時，以時系年。 必書其朔日甲乙，以紀歷數，典禮文物，以考制度，遷拜旌賞以勸善，誅伐黜免以懲惡。 季終則授之國史焉。 自漢獻帝后，歷代帝王有起居注，著作編之，每季為卷，送史館也。 左補闕、左拾遣左補闕二員，從七品上。 左拾遣二員。 從八品上。 古無此官名。 天后垂拱元年二月二十九日敕：「記言書事，每切於旁求； 補闕拾遣，未弘於注選。 瞻言共理，必藉眾才，寄以登賢，期之進善。 宜置左右補闕各二員，從七品上，左右拾遣各二員，從八品上，掌供奉諷諫，行立次左右史之下。 仍附於令。 」天授二年二月，加置三員，通前五員。 大曆四年，補闕、拾遣，各置內供奉兩員。 七年五月十一日敕，補闕、拾遣，宜各置兩員也。 補闕、拾遣之職，掌供奉訥諫，扈從乘輿。 凡發令舉事，有不便於時，不合於道，大則廷議，小則上封。 若賢良之遺滯于下，忠孝之不聞於上，則條其事狀而薦言之。 典儀典儀二員。 從九品。 南齊有典儀錄事一員，梁有典儀之官，後省。 皇朝又置典儀二人，隸門下省。 初用人皆輕，貞觀末，李義府為之，自是用士人為之。 贊者十二人。 隋太常、鴻臚二寺，皆有贊者，皇朝因置之，隸門下省，掌贊唱，為行事之節。 分番上下，謂之番官。 典儀掌殿上贊唱之節，及殿廷版位之次。 凡國有大禮，侍中行事，及進中嚴外辦之版，皆贊相焉。 城門郎城門郎四員。 從六品上。 漢有城門校尉，掌京城諸門啟閉之節。 隋改校尉為城門郎，置四員，從六品，皇朝因之也。 令史一人，書令史二人，門僕八百人。 門僕，晉代有之。 皇朝隸城門局，分番上下，掌送管鑰。 城門郎掌京城皇城宮殿諸門啟閉之節，奉出納管鑰。 開則先外而後內，合則先內而後外，所以重中禁，尊皇居也。 候其晨昏擊鼓之節而啟閉之。 凡皇城宮城合門之鑰，先酉而出，後戌而入； 開門之鑰，後醜而出，夜盡而入。 京城合門之鑰，後申而出，先子而入； 開門之鑰，後子而出，先卯而入。 若非其時而有命啟閉，則詣閣覆奏。 符寶郎符寶郎四員。 從六品上。 周有典瑞之職，秦有符璽令，漢曰符璽郎。 兩漢得秦六璽及傳國璽，後代傳之。 隋置符璽郎二員，從六品。 天后惡璽字，改為寶。 其受命傳國等八璽文。 並改雕寶字。 神龍初，復為符璽郎。 開元初，又改為符寶，從璽文也。 令史二人，書令史三人，主寶六人，主符三十人，主節十八人。 符寶郎掌天子八寶及國之符節，辨其所用。 有事則請於內，既事則奉而藏之。 八寶：一曰神寶，所以承百王，鎮萬國。 二曰受命寶，所以修封禪，禮神祇。 三曰皇帝行寶，答疏于王公則用之； 四曰皇帝之寶，勞來勳賢則用之。 五曰皇帝信寶，徵召臣下則用之。 六曰天子行寶，答四夷書則用之。 七曰天子之寶，慰撫蠻夷則用之； 八曰天子信寶，發番國兵則用之。 凡大朝會，則捧寶以進於御座。 車駕行幸，則奉寶以從于黃鉞之內。 凡國有大事，則出納符節，辨其左右之異，藏其左而班其右，以合中外之契焉。 一曰銅魚符，所以起軍旅，易守長。 二曰傳符，所以給郵驛，通制命。 三曰隨身魚符，所以明貴賤，應徵召。 四曰木契，所以重鎮守，慎出納。 五曰旌節，所以委良能，假賞罰。 魚符之制，王畿之內，左三右一； 王畿之外，左五右一。 左者在內，右者在外。 行用之日，從第一為首，後事須用，以次發之，周而復始。 大事兼敕書，小事但降符，函封遣使，合而行之。 傳符之制，太子監國曰雙龍之符，左右各十。 京都留守曰麟符，左二十，其右一十有九。 東方曰青龍之符，西方曰騶虞之符，南方曰硃雀之符，北方曰玄武之符，左四右三。 左者進內，右者付外。 隨身魚符之制，左二右一，太子以玉，親王以金，庶官以銅，佩以為飾。 刻姓名者，去官而納焉； 不刻者，傳而佩之。 木契之制，太子監國，則王畿之內，左右各三； 王畿之外，左右各五； 庶官鎮守，則左右各十。 旌節之制，命大將帥及遣使于四方，則請而佩之。 旌以專賞，節以專殺。 《周禮》之制，山國用虎節，土國用人節，澤國用龍節，皆金也。 又雲，道路用旌節，即漢使所持者是也。 弘文館弘文館：後漢有東觀，魏有崇文館，宋有玄、史二館，南齊有總明館，梁有士林館，北齊有文林館，後周有崇文館，皆著撰文史，鳩聚學徒之所也。 武德初置修文館，後改為弘文館。 後避太子諱，改曰昭文館。 開元七年，復為弘文館，隸門下省。
The Chancellery. Under Qin and early Han the court appointed Attendants-in-Ordinary, before terrace-and-department names existed. Jin first established the Chancellery; the Southern and Northern Dynasties kept it. Longshuo renamed it Eastern Terrace; Guangde made it Phoenix Terrace; Shenlong restored the old name. Attendant-in-Ordinary: two posts. Under the Sui the title was Recall Speaker; it was also called Palace Attendant. Wude used Recall Speaker, then restored Attendant-in-Ordinary. Longshuo made it Eastern Terrace Left Chancellor; Guangde year 1 made it Recall Speaker; Shenlong restored Attendant-in-Ordinary. Kaiyuan year 1 made it Yellow Gate Director; year 5 restored Attendant-in-Ordinary. Tianbao year 2 made it Left Chancellor. Zhide year 2 restored Attendant-in-Ordinary. Wude statutes set Attendant-in-Ordinary at positive third rank; Dali year 2, month 11, day 9 raised it to positive second rank. By old custom chancellors deliberated in the Chancellery at the Hall of Administration. In Yongchun year 2, month 7, Secretariat Director Pei Yan moved the Hall of Administration to the Secretariat because the Secretariat held the government brush. Kaiyuan year 11, Secretariat Director Zhang Yue renamed the Hall of Administration Secretariat-and-Chancellery and changed its seal accordingly. The Attendant-in-Ordinary received and issued imperial commands, brightened the great norm, oversaw civil offices, assisted ritual, harmonized the realm, and aided affairs—assisting the Son of Heaven in great government. Military and state affairs were jointly summarized with the Secretariat Director: they deliberated seated, then raised and executed—this in broad outline. Communications upward had six forms: memorial copies, impeachment memorials, battlefield bulletins, deliberations, petitions, and reports; all were reviewed, signed, resubmitted, and implemented. On state progresses they bore the seals and followed. At great assemblies and sacrifices they announced inner vigil and outer preparations, setting the rhythm of movement. When the carriage returned, they requested release of vigil to announce the rites complete. At great sacrifices, after the emperor entered abstention and held court, they asked him to the abstention chamber. At the offering they presented jade and silks. At hand-washing they poured water from the pitcher. At cup-washing they drew water from the urn to present. When assisting the first pouring, they advanced the blessing wine to complete the rite. In the ancestral temple they advanced the libation cup and assisted in the aromatic libation wine. After the libation they assisted in pouring the clear wine. The rest followed rites for feasting the spirits. At the plowing ceremony they presented the plow to assist. When feudal lords and foreign chieftains came to court, they received the edict and offered courteous inquiry. At the throne, when appointing envoys, enfeoffing the empress, or investing the heir apparent, they received the edict to deliver the command. For edicts comforting outer officials or summoning them, they supervised sealing. When dispatching couriers and envoys, they issued transit tallies for the realm's communications. Abolition or establishment of offices and titles and changes in punishments and policy were entrusted to record-keeping officers. Once written on the register, they supervised the notation. For sixth rank and below, when offices submitted candidates, they weighed seniority, talent, and fitness to determine appointment. If the proposed post did not fit the person, they weighed merit or demerit and sent the case back. Chancellery Vice Minister: two posts. Under the Sui the title was Yellow Gate Vice Minister. Longshuo made it Eastern Terrace Vice Minister; Xianheng restored Yellow Gate Vice Minister; Chuigong made it Phoenix Terrace Vice Minister; Tianbao year 2 made Chancellery Vice Minister; Qianyuan year 1 made Yellow Gate Vice Minister; Dali year 2, month 4 restored Chancellery Vice Minister. Wude statutes set Secretariat and Chancellery vice ministers equal to Ministry vice ministers at upper positive fourth rank. An edict in Dali year 2, month 9 raised them to positive third rank. The Chancellery Vice Minister assisted the Attendant-in-Ordinary. Whether policy was lax or strict and whether affairs were granted or denied were jointly deliberated. At great sacrifices they ascended the altar with the emperor. When the emperor washed his hands, they presented the towel. After the towel they placed it in the basket, presented the gourd cup, and assisted in the offering. At New Year's and the winter solstice court, they reported realm-wide auspicious omens. Drafting Attendant: four posts. Upper positive fifth rank. Under the Sui the title was Drafting Attendant Gentleman; four posts ranked below the Chancellery Vice Minister. Wude statutes used Drafting Attendant. Longshuo renamed it Eastern Terrace Drafter; Xianheng restored the old title. The Drafting Attendant attended at the emperor's side and divided review of provincial business. For all office memorial copies, after the Attendant-in-Ordinary approved, they read first and signed to correct errors. When promulgating edicts, great affairs required proclaiming virtue and praising achievements, resubmission, and then implementation; small affairs they signed and issued. In great state trials, if the Three Offices' judgment misfit the charge or severity, they cited precedent and sent the case back. When dispatching couriers they examined the business and issued tallies with the Yellow Gate Vice Minister; non-urgent cases received transit documents; where issue was unwarranted, they were denied. For sixth rank and below, when offices submitted nominations, they compared service length, merit and review grades, conduct, and talent; if the post did not fit the person or principle failed the affair, they reported to the Attendant-in-Ordinary and sent the case back. They also examined copying and collation at the Hongwen Institute. Where injustice went unredressed or officials were cruel, they heard suits with censors and Secretariat drafters and rectified the matter. Recorders: four persons, upper secondary seventh rank. Section heads: four persons, lower secondary eighth rank. Eleven record clerks, twenty-two document record clerks, seven arsenal record clerks, eight transmission clerks, six station chiefs, ten custodians, and five edict-repair craftsmen. Left Regular Attendant of the Loose Retinue: two posts. Secondary third rank. Wei and Jin established Regular Attendants of the Loose Retinue and Gentlemen, who with the Attendant-in-Ordinary and Yellow Gate Vice Minister reviewed Department memorials. Later appointments were sometimes mixed; in the south the office was not valued and was sometimes abolished, sometimes restored. Early Sui abolished the Gentleman Attendant; four Regular Attendants at secondary third rank attended at court. Emperor Yang abolished it again. Wude at first made it a supernumerary office. Zhenguan at first established two Regular Attendants under the Chancellery. Mingqing year 2 added two under the Secretariat, beginning left and right designations, all with golden cicada and ermine tail. The left Regular Attendant with the Attendant-in-Ordinary wore left ermine; the right with the Secretariat Director wore right ermine—the Eight Ermine. Longshuo made it Left Attendant Exemplar; Xianheng restored the old title. Guangde year 2, month 5 raised them to positive third rank and added four posts. Xingyuan year 1, month 1 added one post on each side. Zhenyuan year 4, month 1 restored the former four posts. Regular Attendants attended, admonished, and stood ready with counsel. Baoying year 2 edict gave each left and right Regular Attendant two participating officers chosen by themselves; two participating clerks were later abolished. Remonstrance Grand Master: four posts. Qin and Han used Remonstrance Master; Emperor Guangwu added deliberation to the title. The Sui placed seven Remonstrance Grand Masters in the Chancellery at lower secondary fourth rank. Wude year 4 edict established four posts at upper positive fifth rank. Longshuo renamed it Direct Remonstrance Master; Shenlong restored the old title. Dali year 4 edict fixed only four posts at upper positive fifth rank. Longshuo year 7, month 3 edict barred inner attendants from holding regular Remonstrance posts. Zhenyuan year 4, month 5, day 15 edict divided Remonstrance into left and right and added eight posts, four under the Chancellery as left. Huichang year 2, month 11 the Secretariat memorialized: the Sui placed seven Remonstrance Grand Masters in the Chancellery at lower secondary fourth rank. Now they are upper positive fifth rank. Since Dali year 2 raised Chancellery and Secretariat vice ministers to positive third rank, both departments lacked fourth-rank posts. They proposed raising Remonstrance Grand Master to lower positive fourth rank, divided left and right, to fill the fourth-rank gap. Henceforth they should rotate with vice ministers and bureau directors to weight selection. The edict approved. The Remonstrance Grand Master attended, assisted, admonished, and counseled. Remonstrance had five kinds: indirect, compliant, corrective, earnest, and direct. Diary Attendant: two posts, upper secondary sixth rank. Anciently the office did not exist; the Sui first established two Diary Drafters. Zhenguan year 2 abolished the Diary Drafter, moved duties to the Chancellery, and established two Diary Attendants. Mingqing again established a Diary Drafter; then Attendant and Drafter were divided left and right. Longshuo year 2 renamed it Left Historian; Xianheng restored the old title. Tianshou year 1 again renamed it Left Historian; Shenlong restored the old title. Three regular-script copyists. The Diary Attendant kept the diary, recording the emperor's words, acts, and standards for the historical record. Records tied affairs to days, days to months, months to seasons, and seasons to years. Each month's new moon and stem-branch marked the calendar; ritual and cultural objects examined institutions; promotions encouraged good, punishments punished evil. At season's end it went to the National Historian. From after Emperor Xian of Han, dynasties kept imperial diaries compiled by the historiography office; each season produced a scroll for the History Office. Left Remonstrance Supplementer and Left Remonstrance Collector: two Left Remonstrance Supplementers, upper secondary seventh rank. Two Left Remonstrance Collectors. Upper secondary eighth rank. Anciently these offices did not exist. Chuigong year 1, month 2, day 29 edict: "Recording words and writing events urgently requires wide search; yet Supplementers and Collectors have not been broadly enrolled. Shared governance requires many talents; entrusting advancement of the worthy expects progress in goodness. Establish two Left and two Right Remonstrance Supplementers at upper secondary seventh rank and two Left and two Right Remonstrance Collectors at upper secondary eighth rank, attending and remonstrating below the left and right historians. This is also appended to the statutes. Tianshou year 2, month 2 added three posts per side, five in all with the former. Dali year 4 established two inner-attendant Supplementers and Collectors per side. Year 7, month 5, day 11 edict fixed Supplementers and Collectors at two posts each. Supplementers and Collectors attended, remonstrated, and escorted the imperial carriage. When orders or undertakings were ill-timed or contrary to the Way, great matters were debated at court and small matters sealed in memorial. If worthy talent lay neglected below or loyalty and filial piety went unheard above, they set out the facts and recommended. Master of Ceremonies: two posts. Lower secondary ninth rank. Southern Qi had one Ceremonies Recorder; Liang had a Ceremonies office, later abolished. The dynasty again established two Masters of Ceremonies under the Chancellery. At first appointees were lightly regarded; after Li Yifu at the end of Zhenguan, gentlemen filled the post. Announcers: twelve persons. Sui Grand Ceremonial and Honglu offices both had announcers; the dynasty placed them under the Chancellery to intone announcements and set the rhythm of proceedings. They rotated in shifts; they were called rotation officers. Ceremonial Protocol Directors set the hall's acclamation cadence and the order of positions on the court panels. At every great state ceremony, when the Palace Attendant conducts the rites and submits boards for inner stricture and outer preparation, they assist with acclamation. Gate Wardens: four posts. Upper subordinate sixth rank. The Han had Gate Commandants who governed when every capital gate might open or close. The Sui renamed the commandant Gate Warden, fixed four posts at subordinate sixth rank, and the present dynasty kept the arrangement. There were one record clerk, two document record clerks, and eight hundred gate servants. Gate servants date to the Jin. Under our dynasty they belonged to the Gate Bureau, serving in rotating shifts to carry the gate keys. Gate Wardens governed opening and closing for capital, Imperial City, and palace gates and handled issue and receipt of the keys. Opening proceeded from without to within; closing from within to without—honoring the inner forbidden quarters and the imperial residence. They opened and closed on the dawn-and-dusk drum signals. Closing keys for the Imperial City and palace left at you hour and returned after xu; opening keys went out after chou and came back at night's end. Capital closing keys left after shen and returned before zi; opening keys left after zi and returned before mao. Orders to open or close off schedule required reporting back at the privy chamber for confirmation. Keepers of Talismans and Seals: four posts. Upper subordinate sixth rank. Zhou had Keepers of Regalia; Qin a Director of Seals and Talismans; Han Keepers of Seals and Talismans. Both Han courts took the Qin six seals and the Seal of Transmission of the Realm, and later dynasties preserved them. The Sui set two Keepers of Seals and Talismans at subordinate sixth rank. The Heavenly Empress shunned the word for seal and replaced it with treasure. The eight seal inscriptions, including Mandate Received and Transmission of the Realm, were all recarved with the character for treasure. In early Shenlong the title reverted to Keeper of Seals and Talismans. Early Kaiyuan restored Keepers of Talismans and Seals, matching the seal texts. Two record clerks, three document clerks, six seal custodians, thirty tally custodians, and eighteen staff custodians. They held the emperor's eight treasures and the state's tallies and staffs of authority and determined their proper use. They were requested from the inner quarters as needed and returned to storage when the task ended. The eight treasures: the Divine Treasure, to uphold all kings and secure the myriad states; second, Mandate Received, for feng and shan and rites to the spirits; third, the Emperor's Traveling Treasure, for replies to kings and dukes; fourth, the Emperor's Treasure, to reward merit and summon the worthy; fifth, the Emperor's Credence Treasure, to summon subordinates. Sixth, the Son of Heaven's Traveling Treasure, for answering letters from the four quarters. Seventh, the Son of Heaven's Treasure, to comfort frontier peoples; eighth, the Son of Heaven's Credence Treasure, to mobilize foreign troops. At great court assemblies they bore the treasures to the imperial seat. On imperial progresses they carried the treasures within the yellow battle-axe escort. Great affairs required issuing tallies and staffs: left and right forms were distinguished, the left stored and the right issued to bind inner and outer authority. First, the bronze fish tally, to raise armies and replace garrison commanders. Second, the transit tally, for post relays and regulatory orders. Third, the personal fish tally, to mark rank and answer summons. Fourth, the wooden tally, to secure frontiers and control issue and receipt. Fifth, banners and staffs of authority, to entrust the capable and delegate reward and punishment. Within the royal domain fish tallies ran three left, one right; outside it, five left and one right. The left remained within; the right went abroad. Use began with the first tally; later needs drew the next in sequence, cycling to the start again. Great affairs added an edict letter; small affairs sent only a sealed tally by envoy—both traveled together. When the heir apparent supervised the realm, the Double Dragon transit tally had ten left and ten right. The capital commandant held the Unicorn tally: twenty left, nineteen right. East used the Azure Dragon tally, west the Zouyu, south the Vermilion Bird, north the Dark Warrior: four left, three right. The left was filed within; the right issued without. Personal fish tallies had two left, one right; the heir apparent wore jade, princes gold, other officials bronze, as insignia. Named tallies were surrendered when an official left post; unnamed ones passed down and were worn. For wooden tallies under a supervising heir apparent: within the royal domain, three left and three right; outside it, five left and five right; frontier garrison officials held ten left and ten right. Great generals and envoys to the four quarters requested and wore banners and staffs of authority. The banner conferred reward alone; the staff execution alone. The Rites of Zhou gave mountain states tiger staffs, earth states human staffs, and marsh states dragon staffs, all of gold. It also says roads used banners and staffs—the type Han envoys carried. The Hall of Cultivated Literature: Han had the Eastern Pavilion, Wei the Hall of Honored Literature, Song the Mysterious and History libraries, Qi the Hall of General Illumination, Liang the Forest of Scholars, Northern Qi the Forest of Letters, Later Zhou the Hall of Honored Literature—each a seat for compiling texts and gathering students. Wude first established the Hall for Cultivating Literature, later renamed the Hall of Cultivated Literature. Later it became the Hall of Illustrious Literature to avoid the heir apparent's tabooed name. In Kaiyuan 7 it again became the Hall of Cultivated Literature, under the Chancellery.
11
學士。 學士無員數，自武德已來，皆妙簡賢良為學士。 故事，五品已上稱學士，六品已下為直學士，又有文學直館學士，不定員數。 館中有四部書及圖籍，自垂拱已後，皆宰相兼領，號為館主，常令給事中一人判館事。 學生三十人，校書郎二人，從九品上。 令史二人，楷書手三十人，典書二人，拓書手三人，筆匠三人，熟紙裝潢匠九人，亭長二人，掌固四人。 弘文館學士掌詳正圖籍，教授生徒。 凡朝廷有制度沿革，禮儀輕重，得參議焉。 校書郎掌校理典籍，刊正錯謬。 其學生教授考試，如國子學之制焉。
Academicians. Academicians had no fixed number; since Wude the court has chosen worthy men of fine talent. By precedent fifth rank and above were academicians, sixth rank and below direct academicians, with additional literary direct academy posts and no fixed quota. It held the four divisions of books and maps; since Chuigong a chancellor has usually headed it as Hall Master, with one supervising secretary judging its affairs. Thirty students; two collation officers, upper subordinate ninth rank. Two record clerks, thirty copyists, two archive keepers, three rubbing copyists, three brush makers, nine paste-and-mount artisans, two station chiefs, and four custodians. Hall academicians examined maps and texts and taught students. They might deliberate on institutional changes and the weight of ritual matters. Collation officers collated the canon and corrected errors. Student instruction and examinations followed the Directorate of Education.

Secretariat

中書省秦始置中書謁者，漢元帝去「謁者」二字。 歷代但雲中書。 後周謂之內史省，隋因為內史省，置內史監、令各一員。 煬帝改為內書省。 武德復為內史省，三年改為中書省。 龍朔改為西台，光宅改為鳳閣，神龍復為中書省。 開元元年改為紫微省，五年復舊。 中書令中書令二員。 漢、魏品卑而付重。 魏置監、令各一員，曆南朝不改。 隋省監，置令二人，正三品。 隋文帝廢三公府僚，令中書令與侍中知政事，遂為宰相之職。 隋曰內書令。 武德日內史令，尋改為中書令。 龍朔為西台右相，咸亨復為中書令。 光宅為鳳閣令。 開元元年改為紫微令，五年復為中書令。 天寶改為右相，至德二年復為中書令。 本正三品，大曆二年十一月九日，與侍中同升正二品，自後不改也。 中書令之職，掌軍國之政令，緝熙帝載，統和天人。 入則告之，出則奉之，以厘萬邦，以度百揆，蓋佐天子而執大政也。 凡王言之制有七：一曰冊書，二曰制書，三曰慰勞制書，四曰發敕，五曰敕旨，六曰論事敕書，七曰敕牒，皆宣署申覆而施行之。 凡大祭祀群神，則從升壇以相禮。 享宗廟，則從升阼階。 親征篡嚴，戒敕百僚，冊命親賢，臨軒則使讀冊。 若命之於朝，則宣而授之。 凡冊太子，則授璽。 凡制詔宣傳，文章獻納，皆授之於記事之官。 武德、貞觀故事，以尚書省左右僕射各一人及侍中、中書令各二人，為知政事官。 其時以他官預議國政者，雲與宰相參議朝政，或云平章國計，或云專典機密，或參議政事。 貞觀十七年，李勣為太子詹事，特詔同知政事，始謂同中書門下三品。 自是，僕射常帶此稱。 自余非兩省長官預知政事者，亦皆以此為名。 永淳中，始詔郭正一、郭待舉、魏玄同等，與中書門下同承受進旨平章事。 自天后已後，兩省長官及同中書門下三品並平章事，為宰相。 其僕射不帶同中書門下三品者，但厘尚書省而已。 總章二年，東台侍郎張文瓘，西台侍郎戴至德等，始以同中書門下三品著之入銜。 自是相承至今。 永淳二年，黃門侍郎劉齊賢知政事，稱同中書門下平章事，自後兩省長官，及他官執政未至侍中書令者，皆稱同中書門下平章事也。 中書侍郎中書侍郎二員。 漢置中書，掌密詔，有令、僕、丞、郎四官。 魏曰中書郎，晉加「侍」字。 隋置內書省，改為內書侍郎，正四品。 武德初為內史侍郎，三年改為中書侍郎。 龍朔、光宅、開元，隨曹易號。 至德復為中書侍郎。 武德定令，與尚書侍郎俱第四品。 大曆二年九月，與門下侍郎共升為正三品也。 中書侍郎掌貳令之職。 凡邦國之庶務，朝廷之大政，皆參議焉。 凡臨軒冊命大臣，令為之使，則持冊書以授之。 凡四夷來朝，監軒則受其表疏，升於西階而奏。 若獻贄幣，則受之以授于所司。 中書舍人中書舍人六員。 正五品上。 曹魏於中書置通事一人，掌呈奏按章。 高貴鄉公於通事下加「舍人」二字。 晉於中書置舍人、通事各一人。 自魏、晉、齊、梁，詔誥皆出於中書令、中書侍郎，中書通事舍人但掌呈奏而已。 或通事有文字者，別敕知詔誥。 至梁武，制誥專令舍人掌之，兼去「通事」二字，但雲中書舍人。 隋曰內史舍人，置八員，掌制誥，品第六。 尋升五品上。 煬帝改內書舍人，置四員。 武德初為內史舍人，三年，改為中書舍人。 龍朔、光宅、開元，隨曹改易。
The Secretariat: Qin first set up Secretariat Attendants; Han Emperor Yuan dropped Attendant. Later ages called it simply the Secretariat. Later Zhou named it the Inner Scribe Bureau; the Sui kept that name with one director and one chief. Emperor Yang renamed it the Inner Documents Bureau. Wude restored the Inner Scribe Bureau; in year three it became the Secretariat. Longshuo made it the Western Terrace, Guangzai the Phoenix Pavilion, Shenlong the Secretariat again. Kaiyuan 1 renamed it the Purple Aster Bureau; Kaiyuan 5 restored the old title. Director of the Secretariat: two posts. Under Han and Wei the rank was modest but the trust immense. Wei appointed one director and one chief; the Southern Dynasties left them unchanged. The Sui removed the director and set two chiefs at third positive rank. Sui Emperor Wen abolished the Three Excellencies' staffs and had the Secretariat Director and Palace Attendant manage affairs, making them chancellors. Under the Sui the title was Inner Documents Chief. Wude called them Inner Scribe Chiefs, soon Secretariat Director. Longshuo made them Right Chancellors of the Western Terrace; Xianheng restored Secretariat Director. Guangzai styled them Chiefs of the Phoenix Pavilion. Kaiyuan 1 made them Purple Aster Chiefs; year five, Secretariat Director again. Tianbao renamed them Right Chancellor; Zhide 2 restored Secretariat Director. Originally third positive rank; on Dali 2/11/9 they rose with the Palace Attendant to second positive rank and were not changed thereafter. The Secretariat Director held military and civil orders, illumined the imperial record, and harmonized Heaven and man. Within he reported; without he presented—ordering the myriad states and measuring the hundred offices, assisting the Son of Heaven in great government. Written imperial words had seven forms: investiture books, regulatory documents, comforting regulatory documents, issued edicts, edict purport, deliberative edict documents, and edict slips—all proclaimed, countersigned, reported back, and executed. At great sacrifices to the spirits he ascended the altar to assist the rites. At ancestral temple offerings he ascended the inner steps. When the emperor personally took the field, admonished officials, or enfeoffed worthies, at the imperial audience he had the investiture book read. Commands given at court he proclaimed and bestowed. Investiture of the heir apparent required presenting the seal. Proclaimed edicts, submitted documents, and writings for imperial acceptance went to the record-keeping officers. Under Wude and Zhenguan precedent the Department's left and right vice directors and two Palace Attendants and two Secretariat Directors were the officials who managed affairs. Other officials then admitted to state deliberation were variously said to deliberate with the chancellor, balance state accounts, handle confidential matters, or join government deliberation. In Zhenguan 17 Li Jing, made Grand Mentor to the Heir Apparent, was specially ordered to share in managing affairs—the first Jointly with Secretariat-Chancellery Third Rank. Thereafter vice directors regularly bore that title. Other officials outside the two bureaus' chiefs who joined government affairs took the same title. The Yongchun edict first named Guo Zhengyi, Guo Daiju, Wei Xuantong, and others with the Secretariat and Chancellery to receive forwarded purport and balance affairs. After the Heavenly Empress, chiefs of the two bureaus plus Jointly with Secretariat-Chancellery Third Rank and Balancing Affairs counted as chancellors. Vice directors without Jointly with Secretariat-Chancellery Third Rank administered only the Department of State Affairs. In Zongzhang 2 Eastern Terrace Vice Director Zhang Wenguan and Western Terrace Vice Director Dai Zhide first entered Jointly with Secretariat-Chancellery Third Rank in their appointment titles. The practice continues to the present. Yongchun 2 made Yellow Gate Vice Director Liu Qixian Jointly with Secretariat-Chancellery Balancing Affairs; thereafter two-bureau chiefs and other powerful officials below Palace Attendant or Secretariat Director used that title. Vice Director of the Secretariat: two posts. Han set up the Secretariat for confidential edicts, with chief, vice chief, director, and attendant. Wei called them Secretariat Attendants; Jin added Vice. The Sui's Inner Documents Bureau used Inner Documents Vice Director at fourth positive rank. Early Wude made them Inner Scribe Vice Directors; year three, Secretariat Vice Director. Longshuo, Guangzai, and Kaiyuan each changed the title with the bureau. Zhide restored Secretariat Vice Director. Wude regulations set them at fourth rank with Department vice directors. Dali 2/9 raised them with Chancellery vice directors to third positive rank. The Secretariat Vice Director assisted the chief. Routine state affairs and great court policies were jointly deliberated. When investiture books were bestowed at the imperial audience, the chief sent the vice director to present them. When the four quarters came to court, the vice director received memorials at the supervised audience and presented them from the western steps. Tribute gifts he received and passed to the responsible office. Drafting Secretaries of the Secretariat: six posts. Upper fifth positive rank. Cao Wei placed one Communications Officer in the Secretariat to present memorials and review documents. The Duke of Gaoguixiang added Attendant of Affairs below Communications Officer. Jin set one Attendant and one Communications Officer in the Secretariat. From Wei through Liang, edicts came from the director and vice director; communications attendants only presented memorials. Literate communications officers might be separately ordered to draft edicts. Liang Emperor Wu gave drafting solely to attendants, dropped Communications, and kept only Drafting Secretary of the Secretariat. The Sui named them Inner Scribe Attendants, eight posts at sixth rank for drafting. They were soon raised to upper fifth positive rank. Emperor Yang made them Inner Documents Attendants, four posts. Early Wude used Inner Scribe Attendant; year three, Drafting Secretary of the Secretariat. Longshuo, Guangzai, and Kaiyuan again changed titles with the bureau.
14
舍人掌侍奉進奏，參議表章。 凡詔旨敕制，及璽書冊命，皆按典故起草進畫； 既下，則署而行之。 其禁有四：一曰漏泄，二曰稽緩，三曰違失，四曰忘誤； 所以重王命也。 制敕既行，有誤則奏而正之。 凡大朝會，諸方起居，則受其表狀而奏之。 國有大事，若大克捷及大祥瑞，百僚表賀，亦如之。 凡冊命大臣于朝，則使持節讀冊命之。 凡將帥有功及有大賓客，皆使勞問之。 凡察天下冤滯，與給事中及御史三司鞫其事。 凡百司奏議，文武考課，皆預裁焉。 主書主書四人，從七品上。 主事四人，從八品下。 令史二十五人，書令史五十人，傳制十人，亭長十八人，修補敕匠五十人。 右散騎常侍、右補闕、右拾遣、起居舍人右散騎常侍二員，從三品。 右補闕二員，從七品上。 右拾遣二員，從八品上。 起居舍人二員。 從六品上。 右常侍、補闕、拾遣。 掌事同左省。 起居舍人，掌修記言之史，錄天子之制誥德音，如記事之制，以記時政損益。 季終，則授之於國史。 通事舍人通事舍人十六人。 從六品上。 通事舍人，奏謁者之官也。 掌賓贊、贊受事，隸光祿勳。 晉置舍人、通事各一人，隸中書。 東晉曰通事舍人。 隋因晉制，置十六人，從六品上，又為通事謁者。 武德初，廢謁者台，改通事謁者為通事舍人，隸四方館，屬中書省也。 通事舍人掌朝見引納及辭謝者，於殿廷通奏。 凡近臣入侍，文武就列，引以進退，而告其拜起出入之節。 凡四方通表，華夷納貢，皆受而進之。 凡軍旅之出，則命受慰勞而遣之。 既行，則每月存問將士之家，以視其疾苦。 凱旋，則郊迓之，皆復命。 凡致仕之臣，與邦之耋老，時巡問亦如之。
Drafting Secretaries attended service, presented memorials, and deliberated on documents. Edict purport, issued edicts, regulatory documents, and investiture writings were drafted by precedent and submitted for approval; once issued, they countersigned and executed them. Four prohibitions applied: leakage, delay, error, and forgetfulness—thus the king's command was weighted. Errors after a regulatory edict issued were corrected by memorial. At great court assemblies they received routine reports from all quarters and presented the memorials. Great victories, great omens, and congratulatory memorials from the hundred officials followed the same rule. Court investiture of great ministers sent an envoy with the staff of authority to read the command. Meritorious generals and great guests received envoys of comfort and inquiry. Unredressed injustice empire-wide was examined with the supervising secretary and the censorate's three offices. Memorialized deliberations and civil and military performance reviews were preliminarily judged. Chief document clerks: four persons, upper subordinate seventh rank. Section heads: four persons, lower subordinate eighth rank. Twenty-five record clerks, fifty document clerks, ten transmission clerks, eighteen station chiefs, and fifty edict-repair artisans. Right Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary, Right Remonstrator, Right Admonisher, and Recorder of the Heir Apparent. Right Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary: two posts, subordinate third rank. Right Remonstrator: two posts, upper subordinate seventh rank. Right Admonisher: two posts, upper subordinate eighth rank. Right Recorder: two posts. Upper subordinate sixth rank. Right Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary, Remonstrator, and Admonisher handled affairs as in the left bureau. The Right Recorder kept the history of recorded words and the emperor's edicts and virtuous pronouncements, noting governmental gain and loss. At season's end the records went to the National Historian. Communications Attendants: sixteen posts. Upper subordinate sixth rank. Communications Attendants were the office of presentation and audience. They managed guest protocol and acclamation for received business under the Chamberlain for Dependencies. Jin set one Attendant and one Communications Officer under the Secretariat. Eastern Jin called them Communications Attendants. The Sui followed Jin with sixteen posts at upper subordinate sixth rank, also Communications Presenters. Early Wude abolished the Audience Bureau, made Communications Presenters Communications Attendants under the Four Quarters Bureau in the Secretariat. They introduced audiences and leave-takers at court and transmitted memorials in the hall. When close ministers attended and officials took their places, they guided movement and announced bowing, rising, and entry rules. Memorials from the four quarters and Chinese and barbarian tribute were received and forwarded. When armies marched out, they received orders to comfort troops and see them off. After departure they monthly inquired at officers' and soldiers' homes about illness and hardship. On triumphant return they met them at the suburban altar; all reported back. Retired officials and the state's aged received periodic inquiry by the same rule. Ten record clerks, eighteen station chiefs, and twenty-four custodians.

令史十人，亭長十八人，掌固二十四人。
Hall of Assembled Worthies

=集賢殿書院=
The Hall of Assembled Worthies was established in Kaiyuan 13.
17
集賢殿書院：開元十三年置。 漢、魏已來，職在秘書。 梁于文德殿內藏聚群書。 北齊有文林館學士，後周有麟趾殿學士，皆掌著述。 隋平陳之後，寫群書正副二本，藏于宮中，其餘以實秘書外閣。 煬帝于東都觀文殿東西廂貯書。 自漢延熹至隋，皆秘書掌國籍，而禁中之書，時或有焉。 及太宗在籓府時，有秦府學士十八人。 其後弘文、崇文二館皆有。 玄宗即位，大校群書。 開元五年，於乾元殿東廊下寫四部書，以充內庫，置校定官四人。 七年，駕在東都，於麗正殿置修書使。 十二年，駕在東都，十三年與學士張說等宴於集仙殿，因改名集賢，改修書使為集賢書院學士。 其大明宮所置書院，本命婦院，屋宇宏敞。 永泰元年三月，詔僕射裴冕等十三人，每日於集賢書院待詔。 集賢學士。 初定制以五品已上官為學士，六品已下為直學士。 每宰相為學士者，為知院事。 常侍一人，為副知院事。 學士知院事一人，開元初，以褚無量、馬懷素、元行沖相次知乾元殿寫書，及在麗正，乃有使名。 張說代元行沖，改院為集賢，以說為大學士，知院事，說懇讓大字，詔許之。 自是，每以宰相一人知院事。 副知院事一人，初，宰相張說知院事，以左常侍徐堅為副知院事，因為故事。 判院一人，初在乾元殿，刊正官一人判事，其後因之。 押院中使一人。 自乾元殿寫書，則置掌出入，宣進奏，兼頌中官，監守院門，掌同宮禁。 侍講學士，開元初，褚無量、馬懷素侍講禁中，名為侍讀。 其後康子元為侍講學士。 修撰官，校理官，並無常員，以官人兼之。 待制官，古之待詔金馬門是。 留院官，檢討官。 皆以學士別敕留之。 孔目官一人，專知御書典四人，並開元五年置。 知書官八人，開元五年置，掌分四庫書。 書直、寫御書一百人，拓書六人，書直八人，裝書直十四人，造筆直四人。 並開元六年置。 集賢學士之職，掌刊緝古今之經籍，以辨明邦國之大典。 凡天下圖書之遺逸，賢才之隱滯，則承旨而徵求焉。 其有籌策之可施于時，著述之可行於代者，較其才藝而考其學術，而申表之。 凡承旨撰集文章，校理經籍，月終則進課於內，歲終則考最於外。
From Han and Wei the duty lay in the Directorate of Archives. Liang stored gathered books in the Hall of Cultivated Virtue. Northern Qi had Forest of Letters academicians; Later Zhou Unicorn Foot academicians—all compiled texts. After the Sui pacified Chen, principal and duplicate book sets were stored in the palace and the remainder filled the secret archive's outer wing. Emperor Yang stored books in the east and west wings of the Hall for Viewing Literature at the Eastern Capital. From Han Yanxi through the Sui the secret archive held national registers; forbidden-quarters books appeared intermittently. When Taizong held the Prince of Qin's residence, there were eighteen residence scholars. Later both the Hall of Cultivated Literature and the Hall of Honored Literature had scholars. When Xuanzong took the throne he collated the entire book collection. Kaiyuan 5 copied the four book divisions in the corridor east of the Hall of Qianyuan for the inner storehouse and appointed four collation officers. Kaiyuan 7, with the emperor at the Eastern Capital, placed a Director of Book Revision at the Hall of Lize. In the twelfth year the emperor was at the Eastern Capital; in the thirteenth he banqueted with Academician Zhang Yue and others in the Hall of Assembled Immortals, renamed it Assembled Worthies, and made the Director of Book Revision an Academician of the Hall of Assembled Worthies. The Daming Palace academy had begun as the Benming Women's Quarters, with halls broad and lofty. In Yongtai 1.3, thirteen men including Vice Director Pei Mian were ordered to await orders daily at the Jixian Academy. Jixian academicians. Initially, fifth rank and above served as academicians; sixth rank and below as associate academicians. A chief minister serving as academician became director of academy affairs. One regular attendant served as deputy director. The post of academician-director began in early Kaiyuan, when Chu Wuliang, Ma Huaisu, and Yuan Xingchong in turn supervised copying at Qianyuan Hall and, at Lizheng, received an envoy designation. Zhang Yue succeeded Yuan Xingchong, renamed the institute Jixian, and was made grand academician and director; he declined the honorific 'grand,' and the throne assented. Thereafter one chief minister always directed the academy. One deputy director: Zhang Yue as director appointed Left Regular Attendant Xu Jian deputy, establishing precedent. One academy administrator: at Qianyuan Hall a collation officer first judged business, and the arrangement endured. One palace commissioner overseeing the academy. With Qianyuan copying came a post controlling access, presenting memorials, and overseeing eunuchs at the gates with inner-palace authority. Lecturing academicians: early Kaiyuan, Chu Wuliang and Ma Huaisu lectured in the inner palace as 'lecturing readers.' Later Kang Ziyuan held the lecturing post. Compilation and collation had no fixed quota; incumbents served concurrently. Officers awaiting orders followed the ancient custom of awaiting edicts at the Golden Horse Gate. Officers retained at the academy and examination officers. All were retained by separate edict of the academicians. One registry clerk and four custodians of imperial books, all established Kaiyuan 5. Eight book custodians, established Kaiyuan 5, divided work among the four repositories. One hundred book clerks and imperial copyists; six for rubbings; eight book clerks; fourteen binders; four brush-makers. All established Kaiyuan 6. Jixian academicians edited classical texts past and present to clarify the state's great statutes. Lost books empire-wide and hidden talent were sought on imperial order. Stratagems for the times and writings fit for the age were judged for talent and learning, then memorialized. Drafting, compilation, and collation were reported monthly within the palace and examined yearly without.

=史館=
Historiography Institute
19
史館：歷代史官，隸秘書省著作局，皆著作郎掌修國史。 武德因隋舊制。 貞觀三年閏十二月，始移史館於禁中，在門下省北，宰相監修國史，自是著作郎始罷史職。 及大明宮初成，置史館于門下省之南。 館門下東西有棗樹七十四株，無雜樹。 開元二十五年三月，右相李林甫以中書地切樞密，記事者官宜附近，史官尹愔奏移史館於中書省北，以舊尚藥院充館也。 史官。 古者天子諸侯，皆有史官，以紀言動、歷數之事。 到後漢明帝，如當時名士入東觀，撰《光武紀》，而史官因以他官兼之。 魏明帝始置著作郎，專掌國史，隸中書。 晉改隸秘書省，因而不改。 貞觀年修《五代史》，移史館於禁中。 史官無常員，如有修撰大事，則用他官兼之，事畢日停。 監修國史。 貞觀已後，多以宰相監修國史，遂成故事也。 修撰直館。 天寶已後，他官兼領史職者，謂之史館修撰，初入為直館也。 元和六年，宰相裴垍奏：「登朝官領史職者，並為修撰，未登朝官入館者，並為直館。 修撰中以一人官高者判館事，其餘名目，並請不置。 」從之。 楷書手二十五人，典書四人，亭長二人，掌固六人，裝滿直一人，熟紙匠六人。 史官掌修國史，不虛美，不隱惡，直書其事。 凡天地日月之祥，山川封域之分，昭穆繼代之序，禮樂師旅之事，誅賞廢興之政，皆本於起居注、時政記，以為實錄，然後立編年之體，為褒貶焉。 既終藏之於府。
The Historiography Institute: dynastic historians belonged to the Secretariat's Composition Bureau as composition officers compiling national history. Under Wude the Sui system continued. Zhenguan 3, intercalary month 12, the institute entered the inner palace north of the Chancellery; a chief minister supervised national history, and composition officers left the work. When Daming Palace was finished, the institute stood south of the Chancellery. Seventy-four jujube trees stood east and west of the gate, with no other trees. Kaiyuan 25.3, Li Linfu moved the institute north of the Secretariat into the old Imperial Pharmacy, Yin Yun having argued that recorders should stand near secret business. Historiography officers. Ancient rulers kept historiographers for words, deeds, and calendrical matters. Under Later Han Ming, eminent men entered the Eastern Pavilion for the 'Annals of Guangwu'; historiography thereafter fell to concurrent appointees. Wei Ming established the composition officer solely for national history, under the Secretariat. Jin moved the post to the Secretariat proper, unchanged thereafter. Compiling the 'History of the Five Dynasties' in Zhenguan brought the institute into the inner palace. Historiographers had no fixed quota; major projects used concurrent appointees dismissed when work ended. Supervisor of national history compilation. After Zhenguan chief ministers usually supervised national history by precedent. Compiler and straight attendant. After Tianbao concurrent historians were institute compilers; newcomers began as straight attendants. Yuanhe 6, Pei Ji: court officials in historiography are compilers; non-court entrants are straight attendants. The senior compiler shall judge institute affairs; other titles are abolished.' Approved. Twenty-five regular-script copyists, four custodians, two station chiefs, six guards, one binding clerk, and six paper-cooking artisans. Historiographers wrote national history without flattery or concealment, recording events plainly. Heavenly omens, borders, succession, ritual, music, armies, and policies of reward and ruin rested on the Diary and Current Records, then became annals for praise and blame. Finished works were stored in the archive.
20
=知匭使=
Commissioner of the Petition Boxes
21
知匭使。 天后垂拱二年，置匭以達冤滯。 其制，一房四面，各以方色，東曰延恩，西曰申冤，南曰招諫，北曰通玄。 所以申天下之冤滯，達萬人之情狀。 蓋古善旌、誹謗木之意也。 天寶九年，改匭為獻納。 乾元元年，復名曰匭。 垂拱已來，常以諫議大夫及補闕、拾遣一人充使，受納訴狀。 每日暮進內，而晨出之也。
Commissioner of the Petition Boxes. Chui'gong 2, the Empress Dowager set up petition boxes to reach pent-up grievances. The design was a four-sided cabinet: east Extended Grace, west Redress of Wrongs, south Recruitment of Remonstrance, north Communication with the Mysteries. Thus grievances under heaven were aired and popular sentiment conveyed. This revived the ancient banner of goodness and timber of criticism. Tianbao 9 renamed the boxes Submission and Reception. Qianyuan 1 restored the name 'boxes.' Since Chui'gong a remonstrance official usually served as commissioner, receiving petitions. Petitions entered each evening and were removed each morning.
22
=翰林院=
Hanlin Academy
23
翰林院。 天子在大明宮，其院在右銀台門內。 在興慶宮，院在金明門內。 若在西內，院在顯福門。 若在東都、華清宮，皆有待詔之所。 其待詔者，有詞學、經術、合煉、僧道、卜祝、術藝、書奕，各別院以稟之，日晚而退。 其所重者詞學。 武德、貞觀時，有溫大雅、魏徵、李百藥、岑文本、許敬宗、褚遂良。 永徽後，有許敬宗、上官儀，皆召入禁中驅使，未有名目。 乾封中，劉懿之劉禕之兄弟、周思茂、元萬頃、範履冰，皆以文詞召入待詔，常於北門候進止，時號北門學士。 天后時，蘇味道、韋承慶，皆待詔禁中。 中宗時，上官昭容獨當書詔之任。 睿宗時、薛稷、賈膺福、崔湜，又代其任。 玄宗即位，張說，陸堅、張九齡、徐安貞、張垍等，召入禁中，謂之翰林待詔。 王者尊極，一日萬機，四方進奏、中外表疏批答，或詔從中出。 宸翰所揮，亦資其檢討，謂之視草，故嘗簡當代士人，以備顧問。 至德已後，天下用兵，軍國多務，深謀密詔，皆從中出。 尤擇名士，翰林學士得充選者，文士為榮。 亦如中書舍人例置學士六人，內擇年深德重者一人為承旨，所以獨承密命故也。 德宗好文，尤難其選。 貞元已後，為學士承旨者，多至宰相焉。
Hanlin Academy. At Daming Palace the academy stood inside the Right Silver Terrace Gate. At Xingqing Palace it lay inside the Jinming Gate. In the Western Inner Palace it was at Xianfu Gate. At the Eastern Capital or Huaqing Palace there were always awaiting-order quarters. Awaiting-order specialists—literature, classics, alchemy, clergy, divination, arts, calligraphy, and weiqi—each had a courtyard and withdrew at dusk. Literary composition ranked highest. Wude and Zhenguan saw Wen Daya, Wei Zheng, Li Baiyao, Cen Wende, Xu Jingzong, and Chu Suiliang. After Yonghui, Xu Jingzong and Shangguan Yi served in the inner palace without formal titles. Under Qianfeng, Liu Yizhi and Liu Yizhi, Zhou Simao, Yuan Wanshu, and Fan Lübing awaited orders at the North Gate and were called North Gate Academicians. Under the Empress Wu, Su Weidao and Wei Chengqing awaited orders in the palace. Under Zhongzong, Shangguan Zhaorong alone drafted edicts. Under Ruizong, Xue Ji, Jia Yingfu, and Cui Shi succeeded her. At Xuanzong's accession, Zhang Yue, Lu Jian, Zhang Jiuling, Xu Anzhen, and Zhang Ya entered the palace as Hanlin awaiting-order academicians. The exalted ruler met ten thousand affairs daily; memorials and rescripts might issue from the inner palace. Imperial drafts required their revision—'reviewing the draft'—so contemporary talent was kept for counsel. After Zhide, war and state business multiplied; secret strategy and edicts came from within. Eminent names were preferred; selection as Hanlin academician crowned a scholar. Like Secretariat drafting secretaries, six Hanlin academicians were set; the senior and most virtuous became chief drafter and alone received secret orders. Dezong loved letters and made selection especially hard. After Zhenyuan many chief drafting academicians became chief ministers.
24
=內教坊=
Inner Music Office
25
內教坊。 武德已來，置於禁中，以按習雅樂，以中官人充使。 則天改為雲韶府，神龍復為教坊。
Inner Music Office. Since Wude it rehearsed elegant music in the inner palace under a eunuch commissioner. The Empress Wu renamed it Yunshao; Shenlong restored the Music Office.
26
=習藝館=
Hall for Practicing the Arts
27
習藝館。 本名內文學館，選宮人有儒學者一人為學士，教習宮人。 則天改為習藝館，又改為翰林內教坊，以事在禁中故也。
Hall for Practicing the Arts. Originally the Inner Literary Academy, it chose one learned palace woman as academician to teach others. The Empress Wu renamed it Hall for Practicing the Arts, then Inner Hanlin Music Office, as it lay within the palace.
28
=秘書省=秘書省。 隸中書之下。 漢代藏書之所，有延閣、廣內、石渠之藏。 又御史中丞，在殿內，掌蘭台秘書圖籍。 後漢桓帝延熹二年，始置秘書監，屬太常寺，掌禁中圖書秘文，後併入中書。 至晉惠帝，別置秘書寺，掌中外二閣圖書。 梁武改寺為省。 龍朔改為蘭台，光宅改為麟台，神龍復為秘書省。 秘書監秘書監一員，從三品。 監之名，後漢桓帝置，魏、晉不改。 後周謂之外史下大夫。 隋復為秘書監，從第三品。 煬帝改為秘書令，武德復為監。 龍朔改為蘭台太史，天授改為麟台監，神龍復為秘書監也。 少監二員，從四品上。 少監，隋煬帝置。 龍朔改為蘭台侍郎，天授為麟台少監，神龍復為秘書少監。 比置一員，太極初增置一員也。 丞一員。 從五品上。 魏武帝置，丞二人。 隋置一人，正第五品也。 秘書監之職，掌邦國經籍圖書之事。 有二局：一曰著作，二曰太史，皆率其屬而修其職。 少監為之貳，丞掌判省事。 秘書郎秘書郎四員。 從六品上。 校書郎八人，正九品上。 正字四人，正九品下。 主事一人，從九品上。 令史四人，書令史九人，典書八人，楷書手八十人，亭長六人。 掌固八人。 秘書郎掌甲乙丙丁四部之圖籍，謂之四庫。 經庫類十，史庫類十三，子庫類十四，集庫類三。 事在《經籍志》。
Secretariat. It was subordinate to the Central Secretariat. Han book depositories included Yan Pavilion, Broad Inner, and Stone Canal stores. The censor-in-chief in the hall held Orchid Terrace books and maps. Later Han Huan, Yanxi 2, first established the Secretariat Director under the Director of Sacrifices for forbidden books; later it merged into the Secretariat. Jin Hui set up a separate Secretariat for inner and outer collections. Liang Wu changed the secretariat to a province. Longshuo made it Orchid Terrace; Guangzai, Qilin Terrace; Shenlong restored the Secretariat. Secretariat Director: one post, honorary third rank. The director's title began under Later Han Huan and continued through Wei and Jin. Later Zhou styled it Outer Historian, lower grandee. Sui restored the director at honorary third rank. Yang of Sui made it Secretariat Chief; Wude restored Director. Longshuo: Orchid Terrace Grand Astrologer; Tianyou: Qilin Terrace Director; Shenlong: Secretariat Director again. Two vice directors, upper secondary fourth rank. Sui Yang established vice directors. Longshuo: Orchid Terrace Vice Director; Tianyou: Qilin Vice Director; Shenlong: Secretariat Vice Director. One post at first; Taiji added a second. Assistant director: one post. Upper secondary fifth rank. Wei Wu established the post with two assistants. Sui fixed one post at fifth positive rank. The director oversaw state classics, books, and maps. Two bureaus—Composition and Grand Astrologer—each led subordinates in its charge. The vice director was second; the assistant judged routine business. Secretariat secretaries: four posts. Upper secondary sixth rank. Eight collation secretaries, upper ninth rank. Four standard-script correctors, lower ninth rank. One chief clerk, upper secondary ninth rank. Four record clerks, nine document clerks, eight custodians, eighty copyists, six station chiefs. Eight custodians. Secretaries managed the Jia, Yi, Bing, and Ding sections—the four repositories. Classics: ten categories; history: thirteen; masters: fourteen; belles-lettres: three. Details appear in the 'Bibliographic Treatise.'
29
=著作局=
Composition Bureau
30
著作局：龍朔為司文局。 著作郎二人，從五品上。 龍朔為司文郎中，咸亨復也。 佐郎四人，從六品上。 校書郎二人，正九品上。 正字二人，正九品下。 楷書手五人，掌固四人。 著作郎、佐郎掌修撰碑誌、祝文、祭文，與佐郎分判局事也。
Composition Bureau: Longshuo renamed it Bureau of Documents. Two composition officers, upper secondary fifth rank. Longshuo made them Bureau of Documents gentlemen; Xianheng restored the title. Four assistant officers, upper secondary sixth rank. Two collation secretaries, upper ninth rank. Two standard-script correctors, lower ninth rank. Five regular-script copyists and four custodians. Composition officers and assistants drafted stelae, prayers, and sacrificial texts and divided bureau business.
31
=司天臺=
Bureau of Astronomy
32
司天臺：舊太史局，隸秘書監。 龍朔二年改為秘閣局，久視元年改為渾儀監。 景雲元年改為太史監，復為太史局，隸秘書。 乾元元年三月十九日敕，改太史監為司天臺，改置官屬，舊置於子城內秘書省西，今在永甯坊東南角也。 監一人，從三品。 本太史局令，從五品下。 乾元元年改為監，升從三品，一如殿中秘書品秩也。 少監二人。 本曰太史丞，從七品下。 乾元升為少監，與諸司少監卿同品也。 太史令掌觀察天文，稽定歷數。 凡日月星辰之變，風雲氣色之異，率其屬而占候之。 其屬有司曆二人，掌造曆。 保章正一人，掌教。 曆生四十一人。 監候五人，掌候天文。 觀生九十人，掌晝夜司候天文氣色。 靈台郎二人，掌教習天文氣色。 天文生六十人。 挈壺正二人。 掌知漏刻。 司辰七十人，漏刻典事二十二人，漏刻博士九人，漏刻生三百六十人，典鐘一百一十二人，典鼓八十八人，楷書手二人，亭長、掌固各四人。 自乾元元年別置司天臺。 改置官吏，不同太史局舊數，今據司天職掌書之也。 凡玄象器物、天文圖書，苟非其任，不得預焉。 每季錄所見災祥，送門下中書省，入起居注。 歲終總錄，封送史館。 每年預造來年曆，頒於天下。 五官正五員，正五品。 乾元元年置五官，有春、夏、秋、冬、中五官之名。 丞二員，正七品。 主簿二員，正七品。 定額直五人，五官靈台郎五員，正七品。 舊靈台郎，正八品下，掌觀天文之變而占候之。 凡二十八宿，分為十二次，事具《天文志》也。 五官保章正五員，正七品。 五官司曆五員，正八品。 舊司曆二人，從九品上，掌國之曆法，造曆以頒四方。 其曆有《戊寅曆》、《麟德曆》、《神龍曆》、《大衍曆》。 天下之測量之處，分至表准，其詳可載，故參考星度，稽驗晷影，各有典章。 五官監候五員，正八品。 五官挈壺正五員，正九品。 五官司辰十五員。 正九品。 舊挈壺正二員，從八品下。 司辰十七人，正九品下。 皆掌知漏刻。 孔壺為漏，浮箭為刻，以告中星昏明之候也。 五官禮生十五人，五官楷書手五人，令史五人，漏刻博士二十人，漏刻之法，孔壺為漏，浮箭為刻。 其箭四十有八，晝夜共百刻。 冬夏之間，有長短。 冬至之日，晝漏四十刻，夜漏六十刻。 夏至，晝漏六十刻夜漏四十刻。 春分秋分之時，晝夜各五十刻。 秋分之後，減晝益夜，凡九日加一刻。 春分已後，減夜益晝，九日減一刻。 二至前後，加減遲，用日多。 二分之間，加減速，用日少。 候夜以為更點之節。 每夜分為五更，每更分為五點。 更以擊鼓為節，點以擊鐘為節也。 典鐘、典鼓三百五十人，天文觀生九十人，天文生五十人，曆生五十五人，漏生四十人，視品十人。 已上官吏，皆乾元元年隨監司新置也。
Bureau of Astronomy: formerly the Grand Astrologer Bureau under the Secretariat Director. Longshuo 2: Secret Archives Bureau; Jiushi 1: Armillary Sphere Directorate; Jingyun 1: Grand Astrologer Directorate, then bureau again under the Secretariat. Qianyuan 1.3.19: the directorate became Bureau of Astronomy with new offices, moved from west of the Secretariat to Yongning Ward's southeast corner. Director: one post, honorary third rank. Originally bureau chief, lower secondary fifth rank. Qianyuan 1 raised the chief to director at honorary third rank, equal to Palace Administration and Secretariat. Two vice directors. Originally assistants, lower secondary seventh rank. Qianyuan raised them to vice directors equal to other bureaus. The chief observed heaven and fixed the calendar. The chief observed heaven and fixed the calendar. He led subordinates to observe and prognosticate changes of sun, moon, and stars and of wind, clouds, and color. Subordinates included two calendar officers who made the calendar. One chief registrar for instruction. Forty-one calendar students. Five observation officers watched the sky. Ninety observation students watched celestial color day and night. Two observatory gentlemen taught celestial observation. Sixty astronomy students. Two clepsydra chiefs. They managed clepsydra gradations. Seventy timekeepers, twenty-two clepsydra clerks, nine doctors, three hundred sixty students, one hundred twelve bell custodians, eighty-eight drum custodians, two copyists, four station chiefs and four custodians. Qianyuan 1 established the bureau separately. Offices were reorganized from the old bureau; the present account follows bureau duties. Celestial instruments and astronomical books were forbidden to those outside their charge. Each season's omens went to the Chancellery and Secretariat and entered the Diary. Year-end records were sealed and sent to the Historiography Institute. Each year the next calendar was prepared and issued empire-wide. Five Directors of the Five Offices: five posts, fifth positive rank. Qianyuan 1 established spring, summer, autumn, winter, and center directors. Two assistants, seventh positive rank. Two chief registrars, seventh positive rank. Five fixed-quota clerks; five Five-Office observatory gentlemen, seventh positive rank. Former observatory gentlemen, lower eighth rank, observed heaven and prognosticated. The twenty-eight lodges fell into twelve stations, as set out in the 'Treatise on Astronomy.' Five Five-Office chief registrars, seventh positive rank. Five Five-Office calendar officers, upper eighth rank. Formerly two calendar officers, upper secondary ninth rank, made the state calendar for the four quarters. Calendars included Wuyin, Linde, Shenlong, and Dayan. Measuring stations empire-wide, with solstice tables and gnomon standards, had star degrees and shadow checks under fixed statutes. Five Five-Office observation officers, upper eighth rank. Five Five-Office clepsydra chiefs, upper ninth rank. Fifteen Five-Office timekeepers. Upper ninth rank. Formerly two clepsydra chiefs, lower eighth rank. Seventeen timekeepers, lower ninth rank. All managed clepsydra gradations. The perforated vessel measured time; the floating arrow marked gradations for midnight stars and the turns of dusk and dawn. Fifteen ritual students, five copyists, five record clerks, and twenty clepsydra doctors; clepsydra method used the perforated vessel and floating arrow. Forty-eight arrows marked one hundred day-and-night gradations. Winter and summer differed in length. Winter solstice: forty day gradations, sixty night. Summer solstice: sixty day gradations, forty night. Summer solstice: sixty day gradations, forty night. At the equinoxes, fifty gradations each for day and night. After autumn equinox day shortened and night lengthened, one gradation added every nine days. After spring equinox night shortened and day lengthened, one gradation subtracted every nine days. Near the solstices change was slow, requiring more days. Between equinoxes change was rapid, requiring fewer days. Night observation set the rhythm of watches and marks. Each night had five watches; each watch five marks. Watches sounded on drums; marks on bells. All officials listed above were created with the Bureau of Astronomy in Qianyuan 1.
